real_s1.explanation: The unit responds to dog breeds with long, fluffy or shaggy coats (Maltese, Lhasa, Shih-Tzu, sheepdogs, spaniels, setters) when the dog is facing the camera or turned to the left rather than to the right. It is also more active on warmly tinted photos than on cool ones. It likes the dog filling a good part of the frame and being sharp, but the similar units share that preference, as they partly share the preference for frontal views. Its clearest particular trait is the left-over-right facing asymmetry.

real_s2.explanation: The unit responds to fluffy, long-haired dogs (Maltese, Lhasa, Shih-Tzu, Old English sheepdog and similar breeds) shown large, close-up and sharp. Within these classes it is most active when the dog faces the camera rather than in profile. Among profile shots, it prefers dogs facing left over dogs facing right, which the similar units do not share. It also leans toward warm-tinted over cool-tinted photos. Facing the camera, sharpness and large subject size are partly shared with the similar units.

real_s3.explanation: The unit responds to fluffy and long-haired dogs, such as Maltese, Lhasa, Shih-Tzu and Old English sheepdog. It is most active when the dog faces the camera head-on and fills much of the frame. Among side views it prefers dogs facing left over dogs facing right. It also responds more to warm-tinted, medium-lit and sharp photos. The left-versus-right preference and the warm-versus-cool tint preference are what set it apart, since its similar units do not share them. Its preference for sharp, frontal, large subjects is largely shared with those units.

null_s1.explanation: This unit responds to dogs, mostly long-haired toy breeds and terriers, that are shown in profile, especially facing left, rather than facing the camera. The unit is more active on left-facing dogs than on dogs facing toward or away from the camera, and this effect is unusually strong for its layer (99th percentile). Similar units share it only partly. The unit is also somewhat more active when the dog is partly cut off by the photo edge, but similar units share this effect.

null_s2.explanation: This unit responds to dogs, especially long-haired and terrier-type breeds, more strongly when the dog is shown in profile, facing sideways, and particularly facing left, than when it faces toward or away from the camera. The strongest particular signal is left-facing versus frontal views (99th percentile, with similar units lower). Right-facing versus frontal is weaker but in the same direction. Framing, lighting, tint and sharpness show little distinctive effect, and the cut-off and position rows are shared with the similar units.

null_s3.explanation: The unit responds to dogs, mostly fluffy, long-haired small and medium breeds such as Maltese, Lhasa, Shih-Tzu, Tibetan terrier and Pekinese. Within those classes it is most active when the dog is seen in profile, especially facing left, rather than facing the camera. It also tends to be more active when the dog is partly cut off by the photo edge. Size in frame, lighting, tint, horizon tilt and sharpness make little difference.
